Chapter 3. The Many Faces of Identity.
As the investigation moved forward, the question of who Daisuke really was... just kept getting trickier. Each new clue seemed to peel back another layer, showing a different side of the man, and suddenly, the line between truth and fiction? It got fuzzier and fuzzier.
Kido’s search led him to this small apartment—one where Daisuke had lived, but under a different name. Neighbors remembered a guy who mostly kept to himself. He didn’t talk much, but he was always polite. Then, in another city, a former coworker described someone who was quick to help out, but never spoke about his past. Piece by piece, these stories built a picture of a man who was somehow both present and absent... someone people felt they knew, and yet, didn’t really know at all.
It’s moments like this that make you realize—identity isn’t just one simple, unchanging thing. We’re all shaped by what we’ve been through, by who we’re close to, and by the roles we end up playing. Sometimes, the person you become is just a response to what others expect from you... maybe a way to fit in, or even to protect yourself.
For Daisuke, taking on a new identity wasn’t just about hiding or deceiving people—it was about survival. About escaping a past that felt impossible to bear. His reasons were tangled up in pain, and in the hope for a fresh start. But those choices? They didn’t just affect him. The ripples reached everyone who thought they knew him.
Kido couldn’t help but think about how people reinvent themselves all the time. Sometimes, it’s because they have to. Other times, it’s because they want to. Like, imagine moving to a new city—you might pick up new habits, make new friends, maybe even change the way you talk. Or if you’ve gone through something really tough, you might try to leave parts of your old life behind, becoming someone who feels safer or more accepted.
But here’s something to pay attention to: that process of reinvention? It never really finishes. The past has this stubborn way of coming back, and no matter how much you change your name or your surroundings, the real story of who you are can’t just be erased. The people who care about you—they’re left trying to make sense of the pieces that don’t quite fit, wondering how all those versions of you connect.
For Rie, discovering Daisuke’s secret forced her to look at her own ideas about identity. Was the man she loved only defined by what he’d done before, or by the life they’d built together? Did his lies erase the kindness he’d shown? Or all those moments when they truly connected?
There’s no simple answer. Most of us want to believe that identity is solid—a foundation you can count on. But the truth? It’s a lot messier. People change, sometimes because they have to, sometimes because they choose to. Who we are isn’t some fixed point. It’s more like an ongoing story, always being rewritten with every decision, every new day.
As Kido kept searching, he met others dealing with similar struggles. A man who changed his name to leave a troubled past behind. A woman who reinvented herself after loss. Each story was different, but underneath, there was always this longing—to be seen, to be understood, to find a place in the world.
The investigation stopped being just about the facts. It became about understanding what it really means to be human. In the end, the search for Daisuke’s true self was really a search for the meaning of identity itself. And it turned out, the answers weren’t hiding in any official record or document... but in the messy, unpredictable reality of real lives.
